title.narrative: Community Security Initiative-UNDP-IRQ-00129314

description.narrative: Improve community security and stability through socio-economic reintegration of FVFs in Sinuni Sinjar District.

description.narrative: - Design and implement two community security initiatives to re-integrate FVFs to the economic work force in Sinuni Sinjar District. - Implement four community stability support schemes to foster local-level institutional strengthening, and dialogue to promote social stability, security, and to mitigate key drivers of VE in the target locations. - Establish OSIC in two target locations in Sinuni, Sinjar District, with trained focal points to provide necessary referral services to all beneficiaries - Establish an outreach center for women and girls in the OSIC two locations - Develop a best practice and lesson learned document and a policy briefing - Beneficiary satisfactory surveys to be conducted to gauge the level of satisfaction and quality of services provided to FVF

comment.narrative: The CSIP pilots to-date have demonstrated that the reintegration package offered has allowed the target beneficiaries to improve their employability, status, and acceptance within their communities and families as well as their emotional skills to plan their lives with confidence going forward. CSIP has fostered social co-existence and helped to mitigate against key drivers of VE, while also giving the FVFs dignity, self-respect, and hope. In the first pilot wave of the CSIP, which took place in Basra, 87 male FVFs were supported with vocational training, psycho-social support and business training. The on going second pilot in Qairawan, Sinjar supports a total of 103 FVF ( 75 men and 28 women) The pilots also found that the needs of female former fighters and female family members of FVFs should be distinctly considered.For example, early indications in the second pilot in Sinjar which includes female FVFs indicate that their level of resilience to trauma is higher – with 65 percent of the men showing severe trauma compared to 25 percent women. A differentiated approach to enhancing coping skills as well as livelihood opportunities and access to finance will also be needed. There is an upward trend in male and female FVFs returnees in Sinjar, one of the areas left destroyed by ISIL. The district of Sinjar and surrounding areas are considered to have the greatest diversity in terms of different ethnic groups, as well as many Sunnis perceived to be affiliated with ISIL. The pilots have demonstrated the need for longer-term integrated trauma-informed, and community-centric approaches to promoting reintegration and peaceful co-existence particularly in Sinjar.
